CausalChain: Tumor cells -> Secretion of EVs enriched in miR-155 -> Uptake by mature myeloid cells -> miR-155 recruits DNMTs/HDACs -> Epigenetic suppression of IRF-8 -> Skewed differentiation into MDSCs -> MDSC-mediated suppression of T cell responses -> Enhanced tumor immune evasion
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that tumor cells secrete EVs containing high levels of miR-155, which are selectively taken up by mature myeloid cells. Once internalized, miR-155 functions by recruiting epigenetic modifiers (such as DNMTs and HDACs) to the promoter region of the IRF-8 gene, leading to its epigenetic silencing. The subsequent loss of IRF-8 expression impairs the normal differentiation pathway of these cells, driving them into an immunosuppressive, MDSC phenotype that facilitates tumor immune evasion. Simultaneously, we propose that the targeted interruption of EV-mediated miR-155 transfer—achieved via nanoparticle-based delivery of miR-155 antagonists—or the restoration of IRF-8 expression through CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) can reprogram MDSCs into functional antigen-presenting cells, thereby potentiating immunotherapeutic responses. This hypothesis directly integrates each step from the initial tumor cell signaling to the eventual immune suppression and offers a dual therapeutic strategy that is testable with current molecular and genomic technologies.
Abstract: In this study, we propose that tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) enriched with miR-155 orchestrate a targeted epigenetic silencing of IRF-8 in mature myeloid cells. Upon uptake by these cells, miR-155 is hypothesized to recruit epigenetic modifiers—such as DNA methyltransferases and histone deacetylases—to the IRF-8 promoter, thereby suppressing its expression. This modulation diverts the differentiation of myeloid cells toward a myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSC) phenotype, which actively dampens T cell mediated immune responses and promotes tumor immune evasion. Leveraging contemporary tools like CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) to restore IRF-8 levels and targeted nanoparticle systems to inhibit EV uptake or miR-155 activity, we aim to reprogram MDSCs into functional antigen-presenting cells. This integrative approach, combining precise epigenetic interrogation with advanced molecular therapeutics, holds promise for enhancing the efficacy of immunotherapy in cancer.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that tumor-derived EVs carrying miR-155 induce epigenetic suppression of IRF-8 in myeloid cells, leading to an MDSC phenotype and immune evasion, and that this could be counteracted by disrupting EV delivery or restoring IRF-8. The new hypothesis refines this concept by: (1) specifying the mechanistic details of miR-155 action via the recruitment of epigenetic modifiers (DNMTs and HDACs), (2) elaborating the causal chain with clearer linkages between EV uptake and IRF-8 silencing, (3) incorporating advanced technological strategies such as CRISPRa and nanoparticle-mediated delivery to both block EV uptake/miR-155 activity and restore IRF-8 expression, and (4) emphasizing how these innovative tools can be utilized to translationally reprogram MDSCs. Each step of the original causal chain is explicitly maintained but now enhanced with clear mechanistic insights and practical, technology-based interventions.
